newsitem.title: UK: Labuan visits offshore Euro centres, raises profile.
newsitem.headline: Labuan visits offshore Euro centres, raises profile.

text.p: Top Malaysian finance officials have paid a two-day visit to the Isle of Man to explore how the island can help develop Malaysia's fledgling offshore centre Labuan, Manx industry sources said.
Investment managers arranged for the officials to meet Financial Supervision Commission head Jim Noakes, Bill Hastings of the Insurance Authority and Transport Minister David North.

The Malaysian delegation included Chin Chee Lee, chairman of the Labuan Trust Companies Association and of the Matheson Ambrose Trust and Awang Adek, chairman of the Labuan Financial Regulatory Authority and a director of the Central Bank of Malaysia. Leslie Norman, director of the Matheson Trust Company in Jersey who helped organise the visit, said Labuan officials wanted business and were actively setting out to attract it.
"They don't want to reinvent the wheel but they want to grow in a modern world. They have built that financial centre, they hope people will be attracted to it and I think they will."
Another investment group said the officials were on a fact-finding mission, seeking regulatory models.

"There is no official link of any kind yet," said Gerard MacQuillan of Monmouth Trust. "They have been looking at several jurisdictions in Europe -- Luxembourg, Jersey and Dublin Free Port and we had the impression that they thought Isle of Man was ideally regulated."
"The visit was their initiative and they were very happy with the reception they received here," he added.

Labuan, an island in the South China sea off eastern Sabah state in Borneo, was established as an offshore financial centre in November 1990. Recently, it has rapidly built up its international presence, aiming to challenge the established Asian finance centres like Singapore and Hong Kong.

As of July 1996 some 689 institutions had established operations there, among them 52 banks, including all of the world's top 10. The centre has attracted $2.5 billion in deposits and extended $9.0 billion in loans, with most of the business coming from Malaysia.
Some 104 investment firms have moved there from Hong Kong, according to official data.
In May, Malaysia allowed foreign insurance brokerage companies into Labuan in an effort to boost interest in offshore insurance activities, an area the Isle of Man specialises in.
IOM fund managers said despite initial scepticism about regulatory rigour and facilities, Labuan had proved "stunningly successful in terms of the money it has attracted".
"They are selling heavily on the Islamic connection, as Malaysia is an Islamic state," noted one. "There is also a lot of Chinese interest."

"Labuan is stable and is building a name. Some people feel Singapore is now expensive, and it has gone a bit over the top on regulation -- an attitude of "do it our way or not at all' -- and Hong Kong has obvious political drawbacks."
